title: Bias and confounding
note: Bias is systematic error: it pushes results in one direction, and a bigger sample won't fix it. A confounder is a third factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome, creating a false or distorted link. Randomization, blinding and placebos are the main defenses.

read.title: When a third factor does the work
text: Imagine a study finds that people who take a daily vitamin live longer. Before concluding that vitamins extend life, ask who chooses to take them. Vitamin users may also exercise more, smoke less, and see doctors more often. Each of these is a confounder: a factor connected to both the exposure and the outcome. Any of them could produce the link even if the vitamin did nothing.

Confounding is one kind of bias, a systematic error that pushes results in one direction. Others creep in through who gets studied, how outcomes are measured, and what gets published. Unlike random error, bias doesn't shrink as a sample grows. A survey of a million volunteers can be precisely wrong.

Randomized trials are the strongest defense. When chance assigns the vitamin, health-conscious people land in both groups equally. A placebo keeps both groups' expectations alike, since believing you are treated can itself change how you feel. Blinding keeps participants and researchers from knowing who got what, so hopes can't tilt the measurements.
Observational studies can adjust for confounders they measured, but never for ones they missed.

q.q: Why might vitamin users live longer even if vitamins do nothing?
o: Vitamin users may also exercise more and smoke less
Vitamins act as a placebo for doctors
